summary: Reports the state of standardization of Internet protocols as determined by the Internet Activities Board, replacing RFC 1500. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1600.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card that says which Internet rules are official, which are still being tested, and which are retired.

subtitle: The authoritative guide to Internet protocol standardization

tldr.problem: By 1993, the Internet standardization process needed to be formally documented with clear procedures, time limits, and the roles of the IESG in reviewing protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1540 defined six protocol states (standard, draft, proposed, experimental, informational, historic), five requirement levels, and formal decision tables showing how RFCs are processed and routed through the standards track.
tldr.outcome: This RFC became the definitive reference for the Internet standardization process and was maintained as a living document through several quarterly editions until being replaced by RFC 1600.

facts.label: Requirement levels
facts.value: 5 (required, recommended, elective, limited use, not recommended)

facts.label: Minimum proposal period
facts.value: 6 months to draft, 4 months to standard

today: RFC 1540 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1600 as the next quarterly update, and the Internet standards process has continued to evolve.

sections.title: The Standardization Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1540 is the October 1993 edition of the Internet's official protocol standards report, assigned the standard number STD 1. It describes the standardization process developed by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), working through the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF).

The document emphasizes that protocol standardization goes through defined states (maturity levels) and is governed by the IETF's steering group, the IESG. The goal is to coordinate the evolution of Internet protocols as they become increasingly important in commercial deployment. A minimum of six months must pass before a proposed standard can advance to draft standard, and four months before draft can advance to standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the rulebook for making official Internet rules. The Internet Engineering Task Force uses multiple stages to test and approve protocols, with set waiting periods between stages.

sections.title: The Two Dimensions: State and Status
sections.content:
Every protocol has two independent classifications. The state (or maturity level) indicates where it stands in the standardization track: standard (officially approved and assigned an STD number), draft standard (under active consideration), proposed standard (candidate for standardization), experimental (research only), informational (external or vendor protocols), or historic (obsolete or unused).

The status (or requirement level) indicates how broadly it should be deployed: required (all systems must implement), recommended (systems should implement), elective (optional by function), limited use (for restricted purposes), or not recommended (discouraged for general use).

RFC 1540 provides a matrix showing the likely combinations. A new protocol typically starts in the proposed-standard and elective cell. Informational and experimental protocols rarely advance beyond their current states, while standard protocols are usually required or recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol gets two labels: how far it has progressed from experiment to official, and how important it is from optional to required. Most official standards are either required or recommended.

sections.title: The Standards Track and Processing Rules
sections.content:
RFC 1540 introduces formal decision tables governing how the RFC Editor routes submissions. The key rule: only the IESG can submit proposals for standard or draft standard status. Submissions from other sources are reviewed by Area Directors, who may refer them to working groups.

Experimental protocols are handled through notification to the IESG and IRSG with a two-week review period. Informational papers are published at the RFC Editor's discretion. This formalizes the process that was only implied in earlier documents.

The standards track itself has two types of states. Temporary states, such as proposed and draft standard, are expected to last several months. A minimum of six months must pass in the proposed state before advancing to draft, and four months in draft before advancing to standard. Long-term states such as standard, experimental, historic, and informational can persist for years. A protocol can only enter the standards track or advance along it by recommendation of the IESG.

Advancement to standard generally requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability of two or more independent implementations, plus IESG approval.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say only the IETF's steering group can approve new standards. Experiments are reported to the IETF for comment. Standards must work in at least two different implementations before becoming official.

sections.title: The RFC Series and Standardization Criteria
sections.content:
RFC 1540 clarifies that all standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs are standards. The document distinguishes between RFCs on the standards track (proposed, draft, and standard) and those outside it (experimental, informational, historic).

Standards are assigned unique STD numbers in addition to their RFC numbers. These STD numbers remain stable even if the specification is updated in a new RFC. For example, if TCP is defined in RFC 793 and updated in a later RFC, both might be cited as STD 7.

The document notes that no RFC is ever revised once published with a number. Instead, updated specifications are published as new RFCs. This is why RFC 1540 itself serves as the authoritative reference for determining which RFC holds the current specification of each protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RFC gets a number that never changes. Standards also get an STD number that stays the same even when the spec is updated. This document tells you which RFC has the latest version of each protocol.

sections.title: Reference Standards and Requirements Documents
sections.content:
RFC 1540 references the Assigned Numbers document (RFC 1340) for protocol numeric values, Host Requirements (RFC 1122 and 1123) for what host systems must implement, and Gateway Requirements (RFC 1009) for what routers must implement. These companion documents provide detailed applicability statements beyond the one-word status labels.

The document notes that earlier MIL-STD specifications for IP, TCP, FTP, SMTP, and Telnet are now somewhat outdated and should not be used in preference to the Host Requirements and Gateway Requirements RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Other documents list the protocol numbers, explain what computers and routers must do, and describe which features are required versus optional.
